newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK manufacturing expands more slowly in Dec.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK manufacturing expands more slowly in Dec.

text.p: British manufacturing expanded in December for the seventh month in a row, but at a slower rate than in November as the stronger pound undermined exports, according to a leading business survey published on Thursday.
The Purchasing Managers' Survey, conducted by the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS), showed the sector was continuing to grow steadily and prices were still falling.

Its Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI), which is seen as a reliable barometer of manufacturing activity, dipped to a seasonally adjusted 52.5 percent in December from 54.2 in November. A reading above 50 shows manufacturing is expanding.

"The Purchasing Managers' Index signalled expansion of the manufacturing economy for the seventh month running in December as both output and employment rose to meet further improvements in order books," the CIPS said.

"However, although order levels rose on the whole, driven by an acceleration in the rate of growth of demand for both consumer goods and capital goods, the PMI was weakened by a modest deceleration in the overall rate of growth of order books."

This was due to the stronger pound leading to weaker growth in export markets for the second month in a row. In addition, December saw an acceleration in the rate at which companies cleared stocks of unsold goods from their shelves.

Michael Jack, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the survey showed Britain was on track to grow faster than any other major European economy this year while cost pressures remained under control. City economists said the survey, although at the weaker end of expectations, would not significantly reduce pressure on the government to raise official interest rates to prevent a resurgence in inflation.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke is widely expected to have to raise interest rates from the present 6.0 percent, possibly this month, to prevent economic growth from turning into a runaway boom.

"The slowdown inherent in today's survey is due more to a slowing export sector, in contrast to a domestic economy which remains quite robust on the back of rising consumer spending," said David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy.

"The second-round effects of weaker export growth will of course ultimately feed through into other sectors of the economy, but it is doubtful this will occur quickly enough to have any major influence on near-term interest rate decisions."
However, Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, said the survey was an argument against raising rates.

While it showed conditions were improving in manufacturing and would probably continue to do so in the next few months, there was a risk that sterling's strength would undermine the tentative recovery.

"With the strength of the pound clearly starting to have an impact on both sentiment and demand, there is a real danger that the manufacturing recovery is choked off before it gains any real momentum," Loynes said.
The Conservative government, which must hold an election by mid-May, could take some solace from the inflation component of the PMI survey.Prices paid fell sharply in December.
"Some upward price pressures have been reported in recent months," the CIPS said. "However, these upward pressures were more than offset by the deflationary effect of sterling's strength."
Employment rose modestly in December, the fifth consecutive monthly rise.
